newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian debt comes in all guises,even roos.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian debt comes in all guises,even roos.

text.p: The past month has shown that Australian investors no longer have depend on government authorities for debt issuance with a broad brush of supply emerging in various guises.
Corporate bonds, mortgaged backed securities and the kangaroo market have all been tapped, and this trend needs to continue to fill the supply gap from the authorities.
Borrowing costs for corporates have reduced as yield spreads to government debt have narrowed, and this spread contraction need not be temporary, according to Bankers Trust Australia.

"While some of the recent narrowing in spreads reflects the cyclical easing in monetary policy, it is also likely to reflect "structural" factors such as ongoing low and stable inflation and public-sector fiscal consolidation," said David Bassanese, senior economists at BT.

Using Telstra's 2002 bonds as an example, Bassanese said that in the space of five years the spread to government bonds has narrowed from 120 basis to around 30 basis points, meaning that it could now raise debt on relatively better terms.
The Australian Treasury and state Treasury departments have tightened their fiscal belts, leaving a gaping investment hole.

Although the flood gates have yet to open from other sources of issuance, Bassanese said that demand for quality fixed-interest investments is likely to grow unabated, not least because of the strong growth in the superannuation industry.

Among recent issues a A$500 million medium term note programme was launched for a subsidiary of Brierley Investments Ltd, a move that lead manager Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd said was a further significant step in the expansion of the corporate bond market in Australia.
"This expanding market provides a range of opportunities for corporates to raise funds," said ANZ Investment Bank's Managing Director, John Sunderland.
The programme kicks off with a A$200 million issue in March.

And while Australia's home loans war continues at a frantic pace, the securitisation net is widening as banks' restructure their loan pools to produce lower interest rates for customers and defend their market share against non-bank lenders.
Westpac Banking Corp said last week that it is planning a public securitisation offering for the second quarter of 1997 after successfully issuing A$650 million in a private placement.
Elsewhere, Hong Kong based GE Capital Finance is due to price its A$50 million floating rate note in the budding kangaroo market in the next few days.

Lead manager Commonwealth Bank of Australia said pricing would be in the region of 18 basis points over bank bills and that the reception with investors had been very good given that it is only a small deal.

"There are more kangaroo bonds on the way. You won't see them day-by-day, but you will see them literally every couple of weeks going on the signals we are picking up in the street," said Wayne Hoy, Chief Manager Financial Markets at CBA.
Kangaroo debt comprises raisings by foreign borrowers in the Australian domestic market.
